Q: is it possible to directly import an enum field in Python 3? A:

Does not exactly match the original poster request, but related.

With Python stubs for MyPy, instead of this (in stubs, not valid for a loadable Python module):

class E(enum.IntEnum):
    E1 = ...
    E2 = ...
    E3 = ...

E1 = E.E1
E2 = E.E2
E3 = E.E3

Have this (still in stubs only):

class E(enum.IntEnum):
    pass

E1: E
E2: E
E3: E

Came to it here: https://github.com/AlexionSoftware/types-wxpython/issues/42#issuecomment-4962290300

Q: git ls-files sort by modification time A:

I found this post a while ago and have been using this method happily enough. However, today it was too slow for my taste so I wrote this fork-bomb monstrosity. It runs all the git ls-files jobs in parallel. Use at your own risk, it runs at least three subprocesses for each file. If you did this on a sufficiently big repository I can see it bringing a machine to its knees.

On the plus side, it is a bunch faster, took my 138-file ls from about 16 seconds down to 2.

I added the MAXFILES limit; adjust at your own risk.

# FORK BOMB but fast
# for each file in the git ls-files output, this runs
# 2*(number of files) shells
# plus 1 git command
# Hopefully the echo is just a shell builtin command :)
function fastgitls() {
   local MAXFILES=100
   (
      local COUNT=0
      for f in $(command git ls-files $@)
      do
         COUNT=$((COUNT+1))
         if [[ $COUNT > $MAXFILES ]]; then
            echo ZZZZZ TOO MANY FILES
            return 1
         fi
         ( BEEFCAKE=$(command git --no-pager log --color -1 --date=short --pretty=format:'%C(cyan)%ai%Creset' -- $f ; echo " $f") ; echo $BEEFCAKE  ) &
      done
      for n in $( seq 1 $COUNT ) ; do
         wait;
      done
   ) | sort -r
}

Q: MQL5 roaming folder getting too large A:

Here are some files you can safely delete:

  • logs\*.log (general logs)
  • temp\*.*
  • Tester\Agent-* (testing using local agents)
  • Tester\Manager\logs\*.* (local agent manager)
  • Tester\Manager\temp\*.*
  • Tester\cache\*.opt (optimisation cached results)
  • Tester\cache\*.tst
  • MQL5\logs\*.log (EA logs)
  • MQL5\Files\Tester\*.mqd (frames)

As well as the following locations, likely the ones that make up most of your 130 GB, as they are ticks and history downloaded by MT5 (or Tickstory, if you use something like that):

  • Tester\bases\*\history\*\*.hcs
  • Tester\bases\*\ticks\*\*.hcs
  • Tester\bases\*\history\*\*.hcs

I regularly clean these up as a workaround to some little bug I occasionally get when doing remote testing under Wine. They will simply be downloaded again by MT5 on the next Strategy Tester run. Of course, if you are using Tickstory instead, you will need to re-export them instead.

Q: How to write to an existing excel file without breaking formulas with openpyxl? A:

Worth separating two things openpyxl does on save, because “breaking” is usually the second:

1. Cell formulas — openpyxl keeps the formula string in each cell (it just doesn’t cache results or recalc; Excel recalcs on open). So formula logic generally survives.

2. Everything openpyxl doesn’t model — this is what actually degrades the file. On save it rebuilds the workbook from its in-memory model and writes ~9 of the ~26 OOXML parts, silently dropping printerSettings, calcChain, customXml/*, docProps/custom.xml, etc. So print setup, custom properties, and — on SharePoint/OneDrive — the file’s version lineage get lost.

If it’s #2 you’re hitting, save with openpyxl as normal, then copy the dropped parts back at the zip level (an .xlsx is a zip of XML). I packaged that:

pip install onedrive-safe-xlsx

import openpyxl
from onedrive_safe_xlsx import save_preserving

wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("Book.xlsx")   # a file Excel has saved — it has the parts to preserve
wb["Sheet1"]["A1"] = "edited"
save_preserving("Book.xlsx", wb, modified_by="Your Name")

It keeps every non-data part from the original and refreshes docProps/core.xml change-tracking, so SharePoint logs a genuine new version instead of treating the file as new.

Caveat: start from a file Excel has saved at least once — a file only ever written by openpyxl has nothing to preserve.

Disclosure: I wrote and maintain this (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/jonnymaserati/onedrive-safe-xlsx
